historical_timeline.summary: Born into slavery in Talbot County, Maryland.
Childhood on a plantation, with hunger and cold, and separation from his mother, who died when he was about seven.
Religious conversion in Baltimore, after being taught his letters and teaching himself to write.
A year hired out to Edward Covey, with repeated whippings, a collapse in the heat, and the fight after which he was not whipped again.
Attacked at a Baltimore shipyard; left eye injured.
Escaped to New York; married and settled in New Bedford.
Beaten by a mob at Pendleton, Indiana; right hand broken.
Published his Narrative; lectured in Ireland, Scotland, and England until 1847; freedom purchased in 1846.
Began publishing The North Star in Rochester, New York.
Attacked by a gang in New York City.
Delivered "What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?" in Rochester.
Published My Bondage and My Freedom.
Published the final edition of Life and Times of Frederick Douglass.
Died of a heart attack at Cedar Hill, Washington, D.C.

claims.statement: Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey, later Frederick Douglass, was born into slavery in Talbot County, Maryland, in February 1818; the exact day is not known. He later chose February 14 as his birthday, because that was the last time he saw his mother.

He was separated from his mother as an infant and saw her, to know her as such, no more than four or five times, each time briefly and at night. She died when he was about seven; he was not allowed to be present during her illness, death, or burial. He later wrote that it was "a life-long, standing grief" to him that he knew so little of her.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Early separation and loss, in his own words.

claims.statement: As a young child on the plantation where he lived from 1824 to 1826 he "suffered much from hunger, but much more from cold," with no shoes or jacket, and his feet were cracked by the frost.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Childhood deprivation, as he described it.

claims.statement: As a small child he witnessed the whipping of his aunt, and wrote, "I never shall forget it whilst I remember any thing."

At about sixteen he was hired out for a year to Edward Covey, a farmer known as a "slave breaker." During the first six months "scarce a week passed without his whipping me"; he wrote that Covey "succeeded in breaking me. I was broken in body, soul, and spirit." The Narrative dates this year to 1833; the National Park Service chronology dates it to 1834.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Repeated physical violence in adolescence, in his own words.

claims.statement: On a hot August day that year, while carrying wheat to the fan, he broke down with "a violent aching of the head, attended with extreme dizziness" and trembling, and fell; Covey kicked him and struck him on the head.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A collapse in heat followed by a head injury, as he described it.

claims.statement: He then resisted Covey in a fight, and afterwards wrote, "From this time I was never again what might be called fairly whipped, though I remained a slave four years afterwards."
claims.clinical_interpretation: A turning point he described as his own.

claims.statement: While learning to caulk at a Baltimore shipyard he was attacked by four white apprentices; one kicked him in the left eye with a heavy boot, and he wrote that his "left eye was nearly knocked out" and that the eye was closed and badly swollen.

On September 3, 1838, he escaped to New York; he married Anna Murray, a free Black woman, and they settled in New Bedford, Massachusetts, where he worked as a caulker and took the name Frederick Douglass.
In 1841 he was hired as a lecturer by the Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society, and in May 1845 he published the Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Supports his work as a public speaker and author.

claims.statement: On September 16, 1843, a pro-slavery mob at Pendleton, Indiana, beat him unconscious and broke his right hand; he continued the lecture tour. He later wrote that "as the bones broken were not properly set, my hand has never recovered its natural strength and dexterity."
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchor for the modern post-traumatic osteoarthritis of the right hand.

claims.statement: From 1845 to 1847 he lectured in Ireland, Scotland, and England; in 1846 British admirers raised the money to buy his freedom, and he returned to the United States legally free in 1847.

In December 1847 he began publishing his own weekly newspaper, The North Star, in Rochester, New York, renamed Frederick Douglass' Paper in 1851; from Rochester he helped hundreds of people escaping slavery as a station master of the Underground Railroad.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Supports his modern work as an editor and writer, and his community.

claims.statement: On May 5, 1849, he was attacked by a gang while walking along the Battery in New York City with two friends.
As a boy in Baltimore he was taught his letters and then taught himself to write; in 1831 he underwent a religious conversion and joined Bethel A.M.E. Church.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Supports the strengths he names: reading, writing, and faith.

claims.statement: He and Anna Murray Douglass had five children, born between 1839 and 1849.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Household at the time of the episode; no health fact is attributed to any of them.

claims.statement: On July 5, 1852, he delivered the speech "What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?" in Corinthian Hall, Rochester.
In August 1855 he published his second autobiography, My Bondage and My Freedom.
In the final edition of Life and Times of Frederick Douglass he wrote of the year under Covey, "My sufferings, as I remember them now, seem like a dream rather than like a stern reality."
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own framing of the memory, written decades later.

claims.statement: On February 20, 1895, he attended sessions of the National Council of Women in Washington, D.C., returned home to Cedar Hill, and died there that evening of a heart attack while preparing to give a speech at a local church; he was 77.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Recorded as a fact; no earlier physical illness was found in the cited sources.

claims.statement: The project roster lists post-traumatic stress disorder and complex trauma as his anchor conditions. No source fetched for this record diagnoses him, and the label is not adopted as a historical diagnosis.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective label left out of the problem list; the modern episode records his trauma history and screening results instead.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Trauma-informed primary care for a 34-year-old editor, author, and public speaker who survived violence, hunger and cold, and separation from his mother in childhood and youth, and assaults in adulthood: consent at each step and his choice of what to share; the PC-PTSD-5 and PCL-5 read against their cut-points; a structured diagnostic interview by clinical psychology that finds trauma-related symptoms below the threshold for post-traumatic stress disorder, so no PTSD diagnosis is made and trauma-focused psychotherapy (cognitive processing therapy or prolonged exposure) and medication (sertraline, paroxetine, or venlafaxine) are kept in reserve for if PTSD develops and he wants them, under the VA/DoD 1849 guideline; brief behavioral treatment for short sleep and occasional nightmares; post-traumatic osteoarthritis of the right hand after fractures that were not set, treated with topical diclofenac, hand therapy, and writing adaptations under the ACR 1845 guideline and the CMID; measurement-based follow-up with the PCL-5, PHQ-9, and hand-pain score, including an honest record of a missed hand-function measure; and a plan built on the strengths he names: his work, his writing, his family and community, and his faith.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Douglass returns two weeks after his intake visit and is seen by Dr. Morrison, clinical psychology, the same afternoon. He has used the diclofenac gel two or three times a day, takes a ten-minute break each hour of writing, and has bought a wide-barrel pen. The aching after an hour of writing is a little less, about 4 of 10, and the morning stiffness eases within fifteen minutes. He had his first hand-therapy session last week and is doing the exercises twice a day. The gel has caused no rash. He still sleeps about five hours on working nights, writing until after midnight and waking early; he had one nightmare about his youth in the two weeks, after which he got up and wrote for an hour. Before today's evaluation he asked what it would involve and agreed to it; he said he wants to know whether the nightmares are a disorder and what help there is for sleep.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Douglass returns after finishing six hand-therapy sessions. He does the exercises once or twice a day and uses the diclofenac gel before long writing sessions, usually once or twice a day. He can now write for an hour with pain of about 2 of 10, and he dictates long drafts. He had both sleep sessions with Dr. Morrison. He gets up at the same time each day, stops writing an hour before bed, and now sleeps six and a half to seven hours on most nights; his sleep diary shows two nightmares in the past month, after which he used his routine and went back to sleep. He has no new concerns and agreed to today's questionnaires and examination.

He writes most days with pain of about 2 of 10, uses the gel once a day or less, and does his exercises most days. He sleeps about seven hours on five or six nights a week and has had one nightmare in the past month. He traveled to speak several times this summer and planned each trip with care; he felt watchful on the road, as he expects to, and slept well at home. He agreed to today's questionnaires and examination.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Douglass is a 34-year-old editor and public speaker with post-traumatic osteoarthritis of the right hand who comes in the same day because his voice has been hoarse for three days. A cold with a runny nose and a mild sore throat began six days ago, and over the next four days he gave three long talks without a microphone. Since then his voice has been rough and breaks when he raises it, and it tires by evening. He has a mild tickling cough with no sputum and no blood. He has had no fever above 37.5 °C, no trouble or pain swallowing, no noisy breathing, no shortness of breath, and no heartburn. He has never smoked. He has two more talks next week and wants to know whether he should give them. He uses the diclofenac gel on his hand most days and takes no other medicine.

referral.question: A 34-year-old editor, author, and public speaker who survived violence, hunger and cold, and early separation from his mother in childhood and youth, and assaults in adulthood, now has nightmares once or twice a month, watchfulness when traveling, and short sleep. Please evaluate whether he meets criteria for PTSD and advise on treatment and on his sleep, in a trauma-informed way and only with his consent
referral.urgency: Routine, within two weeks, on the same day as his two-week primary care visit
referral.pertinent_history: He describes, in his own words and choosing what to share, repeated whippings in his youth, witnessing violence as a small child, hunger and cold, separation from his mother, who died when he was about seven, an assault that injured his left eye, a mob beating that broke his right hand, and later threats and an attack in public. He has written and spoken publicly about these experiences for years. PC-PTSD-5 3 (yes to nightmares, being on guard, and blaming others, meaning those who held him; no to avoidance and numbness), below the cut-point of 4. PCL-5 24, below the 31 to 33 range for probable PTSD. PHQ-9 5, item 9 scored 0. AUDIT-C 0. Sleeps about five hours on working nights. Right-hand post-traumatic osteoarthritis on diclofenac gel. He asked for help with sleep and agreed to this evaluation
questions: Does he meet DSM-5-TR criteria for PTSD, or are his symptoms below the threshold?
If PTSD is present, which trauma-focused psychotherapy would you recommend, and would medication help?
What would help his short sleep and the nightmares?
How should primary care monitor him, and when should he come back to you?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Douglass is seen at the request of Dr. Pettaway. Before we began I explained what the interview would cover, that he did not need to describe any event in detail, and that he could pause or stop at any time; he agreed. He describes the violence and deprivation of his childhood and youth and the assaults of his adult life plainly and in his own words. Over the past month he has had nightmares about his youth once or twice, and unwanted memories when something reminds him, which pass within minutes. He is watchful when he travels to speak, plans his routes and companions, and is otherwise at ease at home. He does not avoid reminders: he chooses to write and speak about his past, and says the work gives that past a purpose. He does not see himself as damaged or to blame; he is angry at injustice and directs that anger into his work. He sleeps about five hours on working nights because he writes past midnight and wakes early, and lies awake after a nightmare. Concentration and mood are good. He does not drink or use drugs and has no thoughts of suicide
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Pettaway's intake note, the PC-PTSD-5 and PCL-5 at intake, the PHQ-9 and AUDIT-C, and a structured interview today (CAPS-5)

assessment.display: Personal history of psychological trauma, with symptoms below the threshold for PTSD
assessment.assessment: On the CAPS-5 he has intrusion symptoms (occasional nightmares and brief unwanted memories) and two arousal symptoms (watchfulness and sleep disturbance), but no avoidance and no lasting negative change in thinking or mood. PTSD requires at least one avoidance symptom and two negative-cognition or mood symptoms, so the criteria are not met and I am not making a PTSD diagnosis. His watchfulness when traveling is proportionate to real threats he has faced; his anger at injustice is moral conviction, not a symptom. The PCL-5 of 24 agrees. The screening yes to blaming others reflected blame placed where it belongs

Not indicated now. If his symptoms rise to the level of PTSD and he wants treatment, the recommended first-line options are individual trauma-focused psychotherapy, cognitive processing therapy or prolonged exposure, delivered weekly. If he prefers medication or psychotherapy is not available, sertraline, paroxetine, or venlafaxine are the recommended medicines. Prazosin is suggested only for nightmares as part of PTSD
The main problem is a short sleep window from late writing and early waking, not insomnia disorder; the nightmares add a few broken nights a month. A brief behavioral approach should help
Purposeful work, his writing, his family and community, and his faith; he taught himself to write as a boy and regards it as the way he made his own life. These are the foundation of the plan

recommendations: No PTSD diagnosis: record his trauma history and the screening results, without a disorder code

No trauma-focused psychotherapy or medication now; he agrees. Cognitive processing therapy or prolonged exposure, or sertraline, paroxetine, or venlafaxine if he prefers medication, would be the options if PTSD develops and he wants treatment

Two brief behavioral sleep sessions with me, the first today and the second in two weeks: a fixed waking time, a seven-hour sleep window, no writing in the last hour before bed, and a short routine for nights after a nightmare, with a two-week sleep diary
PCL-5 and PHQ-9 at each primary care chronic-care visit; return to me if the PCL-5 reaches 31 or more, if function declines, or whenever he wants
Keep every step consent-based: explain first, ask, and let him choose what to share

consultant_note.follow_up: Second sleep session in two weeks. No further routine visits; he may return at any time, and primary care will send him back if his scores rise
